"Immaterial" is built on a simple logic: the prefix "im-" means not, and the root "material" can mean either important/relevant or made of physical matter. So "immaterial" flips both those meanings. This gives the word two distinct meanings, and both are in active use today.
Meaning 1: Not relevant; it doesn't matter

This is the more common, everyday meaning. When something is immaterial, it has no bearing on the situation — it changes nothing, proves nothing, and deciding the outcome doesn't depend on it at all. It's beside the point.

Think of it this way: if you're deciding whether to carry an umbrella, the color of your shoes is immaterial — it simply has nothing to do with the decision.

Examples:

  • "Whether you like the new policy or not is immaterial — it's already been signed into law."
  • "The reason he was late is immaterial; what matters is that he missed the deadline."
  • "Her age is immaterial to the job — what counts is her experience."

Synonyms in this sense: irrelevant, beside the point, inconsequential, of no consequence, neither here nor there.

Degree matters here. Something immaterial isn't just slightly unimportant — it's so unrelated to the matter at hand that it contributes zero to the discussion. This is stronger than saying something is merely "less important."

In Legal and Formal Contexts

This meaning is especially common in law and formal writing. Lawyers and judges use "immaterial" very precisely to dismiss a point that has no legal relevance to the case.

  • "Objection! That evidence is immaterial and irrelevant to the charges."
  • "The witness's personal opinions on the matter are immaterial to the verdict."

In contracts, business reports, and formal documents, you'll often see phrases like "any immaterial breach" (a minor violation that doesn't significantly affect the contract) or "immaterial differences" (differences too small to matter in a practical or legal sense).
Meaning 2: Not made of physical matter; without a physical body

This is the older, more philosophical meaning. Something immaterial has no physical substance — you cannot touch it, weigh it, or see it. It exists outside the realm of the physical world.

This meaning is the opposite of material in the sense of made of matter (like wood, stone, or flesh).

Examples:

  • "Many religions believe the soul is immaterial — it has no physical form."
  • "Thoughts and emotions are immaterial; they are not objects you can hold in your hand."
  • "In philosophy, God is often described as an immaterial being — existing beyond the physical universe."
  • "Ghosts, as people imagine them, are immaterial entities that can pass through walls."

Synonyms in this sense: incorporeal, non-physical, intangible, spiritual, bodiless, ethereal.

Where you'll encounter this meaning

This sense shows up mostly in:

  • Philosophy — discussions about the mind vs. the body (e.g., "Is the mind material or immaterial?")
  • Religion and theology — descriptions of God, angels, spirits, or the soul
  • Literature and fiction — supernatural beings, ghosts, abstract forces
  • Metaphysics — the study of what reality is made of
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart

Since the word carries two different meanings, context is your guide. Ask yourself:

Is this sentence about whether something is relevant or important? → Meaning 1 (doesn't matter).

Is this sentence about whether something has a physical form or body? → Meaning 2 (not made of matter).

For example:

  • "Your objection is immaterial." → It doesn't matter; it's irrelevant.
  • "The spirit is immaterial." → The spirit has no physical body.

In most everyday conversations and professional settings, you'll almost always encounter Meaning 1. Meaning 2 tends to live in more academic, religious, or literary contexts.

Notice that "immaterial" is not the same as "unimportant" in a vague, casual way. When you say something is unimportant, you might still mean it has some effect, just a small one. But immaterial is more absolute — it suggests the thing in question is so disconnected from the matter at hand that it has no bearing whatsoever. It's a deliberate, precise dismissal.

So using "immaterial" carries weight. It doesn't say "this matters a little less" — it says "this has no place in this discussion at all."

• It usually follows the verb to be: "That point is immaterial."
  • It often appears before a noun: "an immaterial concern," "immaterial differences."
  • It pairs naturally with to: "This fact is immaterial to the argument."
  • It's a fairly formal word. In casual speech, people tend to say "it doesn't matter" or "that's irrelevant" instead. But in writing, legal speech, philosophy, and professional contexts, "immaterial" fits perfectly and carries quiet authority.

Meaning 1Not relevant; having no effect on the outcome
Meaning 2Not made of physical matter; having no physical body
ToneFormal, precise, authoritative
Most common useMeaning 1 — in everyday, legal, and professional writing

Master these two meanings and their contexts, and you'll understand — and use — "immaterial" correctly in every situation you'll ever encounter it.
